title: Behind the Operating Curtain
subtitle: What disrupted this era? What unraveled time? The shadow lurking in the ruins answers: madness.

trails.title: A Clipping
trails.description: When he pulls out the ice pick, don't be afraid. Panic is proof that you're still lucid ... for now.

content.text:
In 1935, Professor António from Portugal became intrigued by a medical study documenting how gorillas became docile after the removal of their frontal lobes. Inspired by this, he successfully performed the world's first human frontal lobotomy, known as leukotomy. The surgery was remarkably successful, paving the way for significant breakthroughs in research. In 1949, Professor António was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his work.

Through continuous practice and refinement, he and others eventually improved and perfected the procedure, even developing a specialized leukotome. However, the surgical technique required a high level of expertise, and as a result, it was never widely adopted.

In 1945, American doctor Walter Freeman modified the procedure, which became infamously known as the "ice pick lobotomy." The technique involved rendering patients unconscious with electroshock or anesthesia, and then hammering a steel pick—roughly the thickness of a chopstick—through the upper part of the eye socket into the brain. The pick was then manually rotated to destroy the frontal lobe.

In 1950, following strong recommendations from psychiatric pathologist Vasily Gayanovsky, the Soviet government became the first to announce a complete ban on frontal lobotomies. Over the next two decades, most countries, including the United States, followed suit and passed laws prohibiting the procedure.

items.text: Behind the Operating Curtain
Central Tower Waiting Area
An otherwise tidy room is covered in fine scratches and small unidentifiable stains. The smell of disinfectant lingers in the air, mixed with mildew.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Wait here a moment.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I'll report the situation and your request to Dr. Merlin.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: However, since he's always busy, I can't guarantee he'll agree to meet you, but I'll do my best to persuade him.
The jaguar's figure slinks out through the inner door.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Now's our chance, Sonetto.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Our chance? What do you mean, Timekeeper?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: It's unlikely that the jailer will let us search the central tower, even in this situation. We should take the initiative and look for clues while she's away.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: I-I see, Timekeeper. I will do my best.
Sonetto swiftly conducts a thoroughly unauthorized search.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Thank you for your assistance, Ms. Recoleta. Without your precise predictions, we wouldn't be standing here now.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I haven't yet grasped the connection between the Die, your novel, and what's happening in this place, but ...

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: By process of elimination, it's almost certain that your pen pal, Aleph, is right behind this door.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Sometimes I envy your decisiveness, Vertin. I'm sure many people have praised the special talent of yours.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Are you alright? You don't seem as excited as when we first entered Comala.
Recoleta holds her gaze on the tightly shut door, uncertain whether she hopes it will open now or ever again.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The all-seeing sentinel of the Panopticon, veiled within the central tower ... If it truly is Aleph, I—

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I don't know how to face such a terrifying and increasingly plausible reality.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Sorry to interrupt, but, Timekeeper, I think you'll want to see these.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Signed "Urd." This is a letter from Dr. Dores.
The delicate signature matches the one in the manuscript folder.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Her handwriting—It's as beautiful as I'd imagined. Who is it addressed to?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "Dear Mr. Aleph ..." Aleph?!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Looks like Dores and Aleph are acquaintances. Or, at least, they've had some correspondence.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: "Dear Mr. Aleph, my apologies if this reaches you at an inconvenient time. I am Dores, pen name 'Urd,' an ordinary inmate of the Panopticon of Comala. I write seeking your guidance, if you wouldn't mind offering it to me."

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: "I heard from the Physician, Dr. Merlin, that ..."

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: You have the answer to every question—a statement which has been echoed by the Idealist and the other inmates.

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: I have something I wish to ask you. What exactly is your role at the prison? Chief warden? A secret backer? An observer who dominates the prison? Are you truly the supreme ruler of the Panopticon of Comala?
They tear open the next letter, eager to read on.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Dear Urd,

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: I do indeed have answers for every question, including yours. I'm afraid every one of your speculations is off the mark. I am merely an inmate who chose to imprison himself here.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: And allow me to point out that your identity isn't as ordinary as you claim. Why is it that you, my fellow inmate and guest of Manus Vindictae, are so interested in Comala?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Dr. Dores, a guest of Manus Vindictae?
A muffled shattering of glass interrupts their reading.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: It came from inside the room. Do you think they're okay?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The jailer and the Physician! What happened?
The door defies any attempt at an answer, sealing all the events from view.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I'm not sure, but it could be bad. Come on. Let's go in and see if they're alright.
Central Tower Surgical Theater
The unlocked door leads to another room, more decrepit and oppressive than the last.
A cold operating table lies in the center, surrounded by scattered bottles and medical instruments.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: It seems we've stumbled upon the Physician's—

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The Physician's office. I should've known. But, is this an operating room?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: As if this prison wasn't bizarre enough already.
Inside the narrow operating room, the jaguar reacts badly to their intrusion.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Didn't I tell you to wait outside? What do you think you're doing, barging in like this?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: We were just worried about your safety, Jailer.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Enough. Get out of—
Quiet!

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: The reptilian complex governs all our fundamental functions.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Our heartbeat, breathing, fight-or-flight responses, and our territory and hierarchy awareness—our primitive ancestors, like reptiles and birds, followed such instincts to survive.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Through millions of years of evolution, we developed the limbic system.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: This processes emotions and forms memories. It allows us to feel—fear, sadness, anger, joy—our behaviors are given "meaning."

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Now, it's the neocortex that makes up more than two-thirds of our total brain volume.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Language, perception, logical reasoning, abstract thought—this is what forms the complexity of human nature. We read, create, perceive. We try to understand both the world and ourselves. We are forever setting goals, one after another.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: And all this—these multitudes—happens within the confines of the skull, in the tight folds of the crowded cerebral cortex.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Is he performing surgery?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Such a delicate and elaborate organ.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Were it unable to forget, what would come of it?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Can this space, no larger than the palm of my hand, truly accommodate dozens of people at once?

At last, the Physician sets down his operating scissors and needle, signaling the end of the surgery. Yet at the same time, the old machine issues an alarm, signaling that his patient's vital signs are wavering.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: What's happened to the patient? It looks like he's dying.
Her anxiety rises as the question goes unanswered. On the screen, the last waveforms disappear, leaving only a constant flat tone.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Did the surgery fail?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Nonsense! The surgery was a tremendous success.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: I have erased his debilitating hysteria and restored order to the Panopticon.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: What are you trying to achieve by barging in here?
The man behind the operating table stares at the uninvited guests expectantly but does not give them a chance to respond.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Forget it. The next operation requires my attention.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Jailer, show them out. Bring me the next patient in 15 minutes.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Vertin. I'm afraid you have to leave now.
Recoleta steps forward, blocking their path. There is a hint of pleading in her voice.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Please, just let us speak with you! It'll only take a moment! I have something very important I need to ask.
Her question is not given time to take shape.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Important? Nothing is of greater importance than my experiments in the Panopticon, outsiders.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: To ensure they continue, the stability of time and schedule is absolutely paramount.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Experiments in the Panopticon? So you really are the controller of the prison, then?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Controller? What an outdated notion—superficial, really.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: The Panopticon has no need for such a power. Regardless of who occupies the central tower—or even if no one's there at all—every inmate is both the observer and the observed, both wielders and subjects of power.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Achieving such a state requires no physical or violent measures; the structure of the Panopticon itself is the mechanism which sustains it. Comala is simply a manifestation of this model.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Once I confirm its feasibility and adaptability, this model can be applied to any functional setting with only minor modifications.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: So far, it has proven to be far superior to any current system of governance in our world—transcendental, even.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Curse it! Why am I wasting time explaining this to you? Time is running out.
The investigator keenly senses the key within his words.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Dr. Merlin, you keep mentioning "time." What exactly do you mean by that?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Really? You need to ask? Even those oily-headed lunatics know it.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: The end of this era is imminent, is it not?
Indeed—the word that was so close to being spoken.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: You know about the "Storm."

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: That's what you call it, is it? A "Storm" that washes everything away?

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: You employees of the St. Pavlov Foundation should know better than I. Soon, this era and everything in it will cease to exist.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: I must prove the feasibility of the Panopticon model before this place is turned to ruins, or something even more unrecognizable.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: A "Storm" that washes everything away? Vertin, what on earth are you two talking about?
The conversation extends beyond even the most imaginative creations of the aspiring writer.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: No one can predict the era to which we'll be reversed.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: I've seen the eras change time and time again—the transformation of this place over and over.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: But no matter which era each of these nine "Storms," as you call them, has taken us back to, caudillismo continues to plague this land.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Dependency theorists, martyred revolutionists ... I've seen them all. You, young writer, are no different from those intellectuals who were swept away in the rain.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: There is no romance in this era, only the repeated cycles of madness and brutality—an endless, meaningless struggle.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Only in this forgotten corner can we momentarily escape the plundering of the marauders and the chaos they unleash.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Although, it won't be long before this place is looted by those oily-headed lunatics.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Just as it has countless times before on this land as rich as silver.
He mutters to himself.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: But there is still hope. Even in a wasteland, we may still be saved.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: As long as I uncover the path to transcendentality, I will find the ultimate answer.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Ugh, I've already wasted far too much time on you! Leave. Now!
The Physician turns away, beginning preparations for the next surgery, organizing his worn-out instruments.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: You heard him. Please don't press things any further.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Alright, sir, I get it. Obviously, you don't want to discuss my novel with me anymore, so I won't insist upon it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: All the letters we wrote to one another, all those inspiring revisions and suggestions ... I guess they meant nothing to you.
Her voice wavers. Rejections, closed doors, harsh critiques—this proves more devastating than all of them together.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But there's still something I must tell you. Jailer, could you please allow us a private conversation with the Physi—no ...

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: With Aleph.
Hearing this, the Physician stops.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: Leave us, Jailer. I'll spare these outsiders five minutes.
The jaguar turns to leave, her face revealing an uncharacteristic sorrow as she lingers on the girls one last time. This time, she offers no words.
